title: Saturation ↔ Richness — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Saturation ↔ Richness's rich face, its first round at Sketch tier, a proposal: for the technical side, a walk from one sine through an EQ boost, a drive and a lean to a blind test of whether even harmonics sound warmer than odd ones; for the saturation experiment, the page's four versions on a bass line in a small mix, named, then costed, then hidden and ranked against what guessing does. Both blind tests state their chance level. The life half of the page has nothing here a piece could test, so it has nothing. I grow when a listener's results come back, or when the page gets a recorded take to saturate. I never hold the entry's words.

pieces.file: Saturation ↔ Richness — rich — the bend and the lean.html
pieces.title: The bend and the lean · from one sine to a blind test of warm and edge
pieces.caption: **Are even harmonics warmth and odd ones edge, by your ear?** Five steps, one 200 Hz sine. One line in the spectrum. An EQ bell, +12 dB, adds no line to the sine (every other harmonic stays more than 120 dB down) and lifts a sawtooth's line by 12 dB: Common Misunderstandings' claim, held. A drive into a symmetric soft clip makes the 3rd, 5th, 7th and not one even harmonic at any drive. A lean fills the evens, and the curve splits into its bend, which makes only the odd lines, and its lean, which makes only the even. So the warmth the section names needs a curve that leans. Last, ten blind pairs: the same note with the 2nd, 4th and 6th added, or the 3rd, 5th and 7th, at the same strength and matched in loudness; you say which is warmer, and the score is set against a coin (8 or more of 10 happens by guessing 1 time in 18). The steps up to the test are also the Teaching Notes' demonstration.

pieces.file: Saturation ↔ Richness — rich — four versions, blind.html
pieces.title: Four versions, blind · the saturation experiment on a bass line
pieces.caption: **Can you hear light from clean when the level can't tell you?** Part 1's assignment, made in the page: a sine bass line with a kick, hats and a pad, four versions from clean to heavy (on a held note the curve adds about −31, −16 and −10 dB of harmonics). Four steps: the clean line; the versions named and matched in K-weighted loudness, the spectrum filling above 90 Hz where no note is; what it costs, about 4 dB of crest factor from clean to heavy, and the trap the assignment's A/B walks into, since unmatched each step up is also louder, by about 1, 5 and 12 dB; then the four hidden behind A to D for you to order and to choose one to keep. Guessing finds the exact order 1 time in 24. A synthesized bass, not the vocal or guitar the assignment names; on laptop speakers most of its fundamental is below what they play.

offers.what: 'Even-order harmonics (2nd, 4th) produce octave-related warmth — the sound of tape and tubes. Odd-order … the sound of transformers.' Measured in 'the bend and the lean': a curve that treats up and down alike makes no even harmonic at any drive (tanh, drive 0.25 to 8: every even harmonic below −200 dB); evens come only from the curve's lean, its even part, and the bend makes only odd ones (both exact to −269 dB). So the claim rests on which curves lean, which the text doesn't say. Tape is the doubtful case. Not measured here, from the trade's own practice: tape's maximum output level is specified where the third harmonic reaches 3% (Wikipedia, Compact Cassette tape types and formulations), which points to a near-symmetric, odd-led curve. Single-ended tube stages lean; push-pull stages cancel the evens. Suggested: 'Even-order harmonics come from a curve that leans, clipping one side sooner than the other, as a single-ended tube stage does; odd-order from a curve that bends both ways alike, as tape, transformers and many solid-state clippers mostly do.' Whether the evens sound warmer is what the piece's blind pairs ask an ear; no ear has answered yet.

'EQ boosts existing frequencies. Saturation CREATES new harmonics' holds as written for one note: a +12 dB bell on a sine adds no line (every other harmonic below −280 dB) and moves the sine only by the bell's own gain at its frequency (1.47 dB at 400 Hz, matching the transfer function to 0.01 dB). The check adds what the line leaves out, measured on the piece's own curve, not shown in it: two notes at once, 200 and 250 Hz through the symmetric curve at drive 3, come out with tones that are harmonics of neither (300, 650 and 700 Hz at −17 dB FS each), −10.7 dB re the notes in total, against −31.4 dB for the true harmonics. With a lean, 150 Hz, below both notes, is among the loudest. A clause could say so: 'on a single note those are harmonics; on a chord most of what it creates belongs to neither note, which is much of what heavy saturation costs.'

Step 3, 'A/B test in mix context', needs the versions matched in level, or the test can be a test of loudness. On the piece's bass line the drive alone makes light 0.9 dB, medium 5.1 dB and heavy 11.7 dB louder than clean (K-weighted, BS.1770, ungated). Suggested: '3. A/B test in mix context, each version turned to the same loudness, and blind if you can.'
